1:
Who Michael is settles almost everything else here, and the answer divides on doctrine rather than philology. Gill takes him for the archangel who has all the angels at his command, that is, the Son of God, the name meaning one who is as God, equal to the Father in nature and glory. He is careful which standing is meant: not the incarnation, nor the appearance in the clouds, but a spiritual presence among his people, which he ties to the Lamb standing on Mount Zion and dates to the destruction of the eastern antichrist. Henry reaches the same identification and makes it the pattern of prophetic comfort: when the prophets foretell the church's grievances they furnish an antidote at the same time, no relief being so sovereign or so easily fitted to every case as one fetched from Christ and the future state. His prince stands up when persecution is hottest, and stood for his people when made a curse for them. Wesley agrees, glossing the prince as the Messiah appearing for their salvation, and takes at that time to cover the whole space between the two comings. Clarke will have none of it: the archangel was ever reputed guardian of the Jewish people. Ellicott keeps the same line, a helper whose presence does not avert the trouble but supports them through it.

On the trouble itself the timing is disputed. Ellicott places it just before the overthrow of the king named at the end of the previous chapter, and identifies it with the tribulation of the gospel discourse, which follows there as here upon wars and rumours of wars. Keil and Delitzsch make it the climax of the oppression the hostile king brings, falling at the expiry of the last week, and trace the description to an earlier prophet, the superlative clause heightened from elsewhere. Wesley alone reads the siege of Jerusalem into it. Calvin declines the particulars. The angel no longer relates future occurrences specially but proclaims God the guardian of his church, preserving it amidst dreadful commotions and in the darkness of disaster and death; the verse has two parts, the wretched period and the never-failing protection, the promise restricted to the elect. The closing clause defines the church, since many professed to be God's people who were not; and the calamities belong to the true church, not the profane nations, since the singular aid named would not have been needed had the church not been most disastrously oppressed.

The awakening of the sleepers is the sharpest disagreement, and Gill names his opponents. He rejects the figurative reading given by a Jewish commentator, a heathen critic and some Christian writers, whether of deliverance from the persecutor, of the captivity, or of a spiritual resurrection from unbelief to a profession of the gospel; he insists on the literal resurrection at the last day. Clarke allows both, that the prophecy has been referred to a future restoration of the Jews and will be true at the general judgment. Ellicott presses the wording. Literally it is many sleepers in the land of dust, sleep standing for death and dust for the grave; the difficulty is many where all was expected, and he reports a father explaining many as all, but prefers a contrast between the many who sleep and the few alive and remaining. The passage teaches a general resurrection already revealed by this prophet's contemporary. Calvin asks why the angel leaps from the beginning of gospel preaching to the final day without treating the interval, and answers that the two are fitly joined: no source of salvation is met with on earth, so the hope cannot be conceived before the elect raise their minds to the second coming. The church is like a dead body until it rises, the same truth an apostle delivers in saying we are dead and our life is hidden.
3:
Who the wise are is the first question, and the readings run from doctrinal to historical. Gill takes them for the wise not in natural things but in spiritual, knowing their own impurity, the insufficiency of their righteousness, and Christ crucified; at the resurrection they shine in body and soul alike, the body fashioned like his glorious body. Clarke has them thoroughly instructed in Christ's word, distinguished by the holiness of their lives and the purity of their creed, those who turn many to righteousness being those whose preaching converts their brethren. Keil and Delitzsch keep the reference inside the book. The term looks back to the previous chapter and is not limited to teachers but denotes the intelligent, who by word and deed awakened their contemporaries to fidelity during the tribulation, some sealing their testimony in war with their blood; the angel closes his announcement of the future with that thought. Ellicott makes the same identification, defines their wisdom as covenant faithfulness that set a bright example, and calls the whole a consolation for those who will witness the tribulation of the last days.

Calvin approaches the word grammatically. It means endued with intellect; some take it transitively, probably rightly here since the office of justifying is presently assigned to these prudent ones, though the other sense suits the previous chapter better. He then draws the use: the angel confirms what was said of the final resurrection and shows how its fruits are enjoyed, since eternal glory is laid up in heaven, so we should not complain when we seem to suffer harshness at God's hands.

On the sealing of the book they divide about what the command is for. Gill takes it as concealment from the profane who would only burlesque it, and a charge to keep it as a treasure committed to his care; the saints were not forbidden to read it, but he was not to interpret it, and it was to stay secret until its accomplishment drew near. Wesley states the rule governing such orders: the book was sealed because it would be long before the words were fulfilled, whereas prophecies shortly to be fulfilled were forbidden to be sealed. Keil and Delitzsch ask the extent of the words, which can only be the angel's announcements with the preceding appearance, the revelation named at the head of the section. Ellicott gives a different account of the purpose: the book must be put somewhere safe because the need of it will be felt in the time of the end, when fulfilment makes the meaning unambiguous. Clarke adds an antiquarian note: among the ancients those were said to seal who in reading stamped the places of which they were doubtful, to keep them in memory and return to them; he cites a scholar proving the custom from a Greek lexicographer.

The running to and fro is read favourably by all four who touch it, one of them against the tradition. Clarke has many searching out the sense, knowledge increasing by that means though the meaning will not be known until the events take place. Ellicott supports the same sense philologically, the verb being used elsewhere of searching after knowledge and of the eyes of the Lord ranging the earth. Wesley has them search the prophecies and know the signs of the times, waiting on God in his judgments, chiefly in gospel times. Calvin reports the received explanation, that many would be unworthy to receive the prophecy so that it was closed and delivered enigmatically to a few, and rejects it: the Spirit has a different intention, and the angel's advice is that there is no reason for despondency because few receive it, since it remains a precious treasure though despised. The time of the end, he notes, is fixed beforehand by God's counsel, and the verb need not be taken in a bad sense.
5:
The scene changes and the expositors first ask why. Keil and Delitzsch put it structurally: the revelation might have concluded at the sealing, as an earlier vision in this book ends with a similar direction, but then the disclosure about the times of the events prophesied, which the prophet might have expected by analogy, would have been wanting; it is given in what follows, and in a very solemn way, the appearance seen until now being changed. Henry frames it as two questions. The prophet had been made to foresee the revolutions of states and kingdoms so far as the Israel of God was concerned in them, and with them trying times for the church, a prospect that filled him with concern; two questions were proper on that head, when the end shall be and what the end shall be, and both are asked and answered in the close of the book, added for abundant satisfaction though the comforts already prescribed might seem enough.

Who the two are is admitted on all sides to be beyond recovery. Gill takes them for angels besides the one who had given the long account, unnoticed while the prophet attended to it and now seen standing as ministering spirits ready to execute orders. Clarke says probably two angels, that we know no more of them unless they are those called saints in an earlier chapter, and that the river was most likely the Tigris. Ellicott reasons that the absence of the article shows the prophet had not seen them before, reports that a Latin father supposed them the angels of Persia and Greece, and says it is impossible to identify them. On the river he is more particular: it is the stream named earlier, though a different word is used, one generally employed of the Nile. Calvin agrees on the river and turns to the prophet's own state of mind, since the narrative would not have produced confidence had he not applied his mind seriously to these mysteries; his mind was completely calm and ready to receive.

The man clothed in linen provokes the sharpest division in the tile, and it is a division about identity. Gill takes him for Christ, appearing in human form as a presage of the incarnation and clothed in linen to express the priestly office and the purity that qualified him for it; he leaves open which angel spoke and on which bank, supposing each spoke in turn and joined in the same request. Clarke makes him Gabriel in human form, as in an earlier chapter. Keil and Delitzsch decline the identification but settle the reference: the article and the clothing point him out as the person of that chapter, and he is by no means now first coming into view, which confirms their conclusion that he had been visible to the prophet alone.

Who asks the question is disputed on the same verse. Ellicott says the speaker is evidently one of the two just mentioned, but records that the Greek version and a Latin father suppose the prophet himself to address the man clothed in white linen. He then makes the most of the man's position, which he calls striking: he appears upon, or by the margin from above, hovering over the waters. If streams are emblems of nationalities, as they frequently are in the symbolical language of scripture, this river represents the Persian empire, in the third year of which the vision came, and the hovering implies power over it. Keil and Delitzsch note the same standing above the waters without drawing the inference. Calvin summarises what follows before expounding it: the one asked swore with hands raised to heaven by the living God that no prediction was in vain, since the truth would be evident in its own period and men must wait for it.
7:
The raised hands are read as a legal gesture, and the doubling is what everyone notices. Ellicott states the rule: a person swearing generally lifted the right hand only, and both are raised here to give the words greater importance. Calvin says the same and corrects a rival reading: those who take the action for a symbol of power are mistaken, since the prophet meant the usual manner of swearing, so that raising both, as if doubling the oath, is stronger. Wesley agrees the hands were held up for the more solemn confirmation, and adds that the gesture denotes the unchangeableness of God's decrees, for good to the church and for evil to her enemies. Gill fixes the speaker as Christ in human form, high priest and mediator, speaking clearly enough for the prophet to hear. Clarke notes only that the man stood on the water, and finds the description very like that of the angel in the apocalypse, where the same measure of time seems referred to.

That measure is where the readings part. Wesley resolves it as a year, two years and half a year, and lists the equivalents met elsewhere: forty-two months, and twelve hundred and sixty days. Clarke gives the same span but calls it prophetic time answering to twelve hundred and sixty years. Ellicott refers to the earlier chapter where the phrase first appears and rules out a whole school: any reference to the persecution under the Greek king is impossible, given the difference between the measures of time. On the verb rendered scatter, the ancient versions, though not the Greek, understood the dispersion of Israel.

The prophet's admission that he did not understand is taken by all as candour. Gill says he heard the answer but did not understand it, which he ingenuously confesses, not knowing what kind of time was meant or when it would end. Ellicott is precise about what failed: the question seemed to have had no reply, since it asked how long the end should continue and the answer was only the obscure words; in the next question the prophet turns to the wonders already named and, using a different word for end, asks which comes immediately before the end of all things. Calvin makes the confession a credential. The prophet asks in imitation of the angel, having heard one inquire of another; and by the word hearing he witnesses to the absence of ignorance, sloth or contempt, since many depart with no perception of a subject however well explained.

The dismissal is read as refusal and comfort at once. Keil and Delitzsch call it quieting and at once a refusal to answer, yet not wholly a refusal, as the following verses show; what is disclosed there makes plain that the end is not so revealed that men can know it beforehand. Ellicott glosses go thy way as be at peace, observes that nothing further is explained and the prophet is only assured the end will come, and compares a gentle rebuke given to a disciple who wished to see further into the future than was fitting. Gill canvasses three senses: attend to the affairs of the court and ask no more; or write the visions in a book to transmit to posterity; or go the way of all flesh, since a full revelation was not to be expected in the present state. Calvin says the wish was pious and contained nothing unlawful, but God, knowing what was good for him, did not grant it, wishing some predictions partially understood and the rest concealed until the full period of revelation arrived; the angel, he notes, now uses seal in another sense. Clarke, on the same clause, ventures a calculation: the time of the end will not arrive before the twentieth century. Wesley leaves it at a line: they shall not be clearly understood till the event makes them good.
10:
The purification is read as the answer given in place of the one asked for. Gill puts it that way outright: since no explicit answer was given about when the church's troubles would end, the use of them is pointed out instead, which duly considered would help the saints endure with more patience, many being made purer and their corruptions weakened. Keil and Delitzsch derive the clause from the previous chapter and say the purifying is effected through the tribulation endured to the end, the prophecy itself serving that object, though not all attain it, since the ungodly remain ungodly and never come to understand the words. Clarke describes the same work carried on during the interim, men purified in the midst of trials, while the eyes of the wicked are closed and their hearts hardened because they continue in their sins, and those who open their hearts to God receive light. Ellicott takes the words as a guarantee that all shall be fulfilled, the persecution certainly arising, the righteous purified and the wicked becoming apostates, the wise and they only understanding the profit of tribulation. Wesley compresses the image: the afflictions prepare the church by taking away her filth as gold and silver are refined. Calvin supplies the motive: the persecutions are announced to arm the faithful for the coming conflicts, since our minds are naturally weak and fall down lifeless through terror as soon as a cause of fear arises, before it comes to blows, so that our imbecility requires many stimulants to patience.

The numbered days are the hardest passage in the chapter and nobody hides it. Ellicott says the prophecy appears here to recur to the more immediate future, the language about the abomination being almost verbally identical with three earlier passages; and he names the trouble plainly, calling the relation of the two longer numbers to the twenty-three hundred days, and to the time, times and a half, a great and apparently insoluble difficulty. Keil and Delitzsch take the opposite view: the words point back so distinctly to a passage in the previous chapter that they must be referred, as there, to the desecration under the Greek king. Calvin denies exactly that. The obscurity has caused the passage to be twisted in a variety of ways; he showed at the end of an earlier chapter why it cannot refer to the profanation under that king, and holds that the angel here witnesses to a destruction so complete as to leave no room for hope of restoration. Clarke declines the quarrel by making the phrase proverbial, applicable to anything substituted for or set against the ordinances of God, and instances a pagan temple built on the site of the Jerusalem temple and a great church turned into a mosque, before suggesting a whole religion as the abomination. Gill allegorizes: the daily sacrifice is the doctrine of atonement by the sacrifice of Christ, taken away by antichrist at his height when the doctrine of works was established and the merits of men set against Christ's.

On the second and longer number the same division holds. Gill makes the extra forty-five a span of years in which the vials are poured on the antichristian states and the Turkish empire destroyed, clearing the way for the visible kingdom. Clarke computes the difference, seventy-five days more than the three and a half years of the earlier verse, and applies the principle of a day for a year to make it thirteen hundred and thirty-five years. Ellicott gives the last words their plainest sense: the prophet shall rest in the grave and stand up in his own lot at the end of the days. Keil and Delitzsch read the dismissal as the angel releasing a highly favoured prophet from his life's work with a comforting assurance, and reject two proposed renderings of the phrase.
13:
The dismissal is taken by all five as a word about death, and they differ chiefly in how much they build on it. Gill states it barely: prepare for death and expect to be under its power, lying in the grave until the end of the world and the resurrection morning. Wesley gives the same sense a purpose, that these things were revealed so the prophet and his people might be prepared for sufferings and yet not left without hope of a glorious deliverance; in that hope he shall die and rest from trouble till the resurrection of the just. He draws the application outward, that it ought to be the great concern of every one of us to secure a happy lot in the end of the days, after which we may well be content with our present lot and welcome the will of God.

Calvin reads the command as announcement rather than order. The angel repeats what he had said before, that the full time of perfect light had not yet arrived because God wished to hold the minds of his people in suspense until the manifestation of Christ; so the prophet is told to be content with his lot, the complete manifestation of the prophecy being put off to a time God alone knows to be fitting. On the two verbs he differs from other translators: the angel does not seem to be commanding what he wishes done but announcing what will happen, as if to say, thou shalt rest, meaning thou shalt die, and then thou shalt stand, meaning thy death shall not be complete destruction. God will cause him to stand in his lot with the rest of the elect, after the patience of his people has been sufficiently proved and the church humbled and purged by long and numberless contests, though a time of repose must necessarily intervene first.

Ellicott alone chases the figure behind the word lot, and finds it in the history rather than in the eschatology. The reference is to the partition of Palestine by lot in the days of Joshua, and even so shall one greater than Joshua divide the heavenly Canaan among the saints who follow this prophet in faith, firmness and consistency.

Clarke turns the last verse into four heads of advice and addresses them to the reader rather than to the prophet. Thou hast a way, a walk in life which God has assigned thee; walk in it, for it is thine. There will be an end to thee of all earthly things, death being at the door and eternity at hand, so go on to the end and be faithful unto death. There is a rest provided for the people of God, for the body in the grave and for the soul in the divine favour here and finally in paradise. And as in the promised land there was a lot for each of God's people, so in heaven there is a lot for thee: do not lose it, do not sell it, do not let thy enemy rob thee of it, but be determined to stand in thine own lot at the end of the days, keeping the faith and dying in the Lord that thou mayest rise and reign with him.
